searched: Read package.json, playwright.config.ts, vitest.config.ts, netlify.toml, deploy.sh, _rules/CODE_SAFETY.md, all 5 files in .github/workflows/ (quality.yml, invariants.yml, db-migrate.yml, inventory-freshness.yml, cron-jobs.yml), scripts/api-smoke.ts, scripts/e2e-booking.ts (header comments + first 50 lines), lib/feature-flags.ts (full file), supabase/migrations/028_feature_flags.sql plus every migration that inserts into feature_flags (grep), app/api/admin/feature-flags/route.ts, _backend-system/README.md (confirms the 15-topic scope has no testing/release/CI topic), _backend-system/research/migrations.md and _backend-system/audit/migrations.md (to avoid duplicating that domain's migration-technique findings), _docs/BACKEND.md headings, e2e/visual/*.spec.ts, _design-system/REMOVED.md. Ran `find`/`wc` to count real test files (8: 6 vitest + 2 playwright) versus 21 ad-hoc scripts/*-kill-test.ts scripts versus 203 pages / 357 API routes. Ran `git log` on quality.yml history and `gh secret list` (read-only, succeeded) against the live GitHub repo to verify which CI secrets are actually configured today. `gh api` calls for branch-protection/workflow-run history failed on a sandbox TLS restriction, so branch-protection status is NOT claimed as a finding (unverifiable from here, not asserted either way).

findings.title: The one E2E test that matters has never actually run in CI
findings.principle: Any CI job gated on `if secrets present` must fail loud (non-zero exit, red check) when the required secrets are absent for more than one release cycle, never silently report SUCCESS. A job whose entire body is skippable by a missing secret is not a test, it is a placebo.
findings.why: A CI check that can pass by doing nothing is worse than no check: it produces false confidence that the money path is protected, so a real regression in booking-create/pay-intent/cancel ships to the 28 live salons with a green checkmark next to it.
findings.local_evidence: .github/workflows/quality.yml's `e2e` job (lines defining `secrets-check`) requires SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY, NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL, NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY, and STRIPE_SECRET_KEY all present, else it prints a warning and every subsequent step is individually skipped, so the job still reports SUCCESS. `gh secret list` against the live repo (sulo232/solen) returned exactly 4 secrets: CRON_SECRET, NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY, NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL, SUPABASE_SERVICE_ROLE_KEY. STRIPE_SECRET_KEY is absent. scripts/e2e-booking.ts (461 lines) is a real, carefully self-cleaning test that drives the actual create -> pay-intent -> cancel route handlers against the sanctioned test salon with a real Stripe TEST PaymentIntent, and its own header documents it was built and passing '22/22 twice' at commit 53c1890ea. Since that commit, it has had zero chances to run for real in CI because the one secret it needs was never added.
findings.absence_proof: grep -rn 'smoke\|e2e' .github/workflows/*.yml shows only quality.yml referencing `npm run e2e`, gated as described. `gh secret list` (live, read-only) confirms STRIPE_SECRET_KEY is not set. No workflow or doc anywhere states a deadline or alert for 'this job has been silently skipping for N weeks.'
findings.existing_coverage: partial: the job's own YAML comment names the exact `gh secret set STRIPE_SECRET_KEY` one-liner needed to activate it, so the author knew the gap and left it for the owner. No enforcement or expiry exists to stop it staying dark indefinitely.
findings.where_it_should_live: _backend-system/LAW.md or a new _rules/RELEASE.md; the immediate fix is operational, not a doc (set the secret), but the LAW belongs at the CI-design level so the next gated job doesn't repeat this.
findings.enforcement: gate: a scheduled or PR-triggered check that fails the build if a job's secrets-check has resolved to false for more than, say, 2 weeks (a small script reading `gh run list` / workflow annotations); at minimum, change the `::warning::` to `::error::` after a stated grace period so a permanently-dark test job cannot stay invisible.

findings.title: No rollback procedure exists for a bad production deploy
findings.principle: Every release channel this product ships through (Netlify web deploys, Supabase migrations, GitHub Actions crons) must have one written, named rollback action, and it must be findable in under 30 seconds by a session that has never seen this repo before. For Netlify specifically: 'open Netlify -> Deploys -> find the last known-good deploy -> Publish deploy' reverts the live site to a prior atomic build in under a minute with no code change, and this must be written down, not rediscovered under pressure.
findings.why: At 28 salons, a bad deploy is rare but the FIRST time it happens is exactly when nobody should be improvising a recovery plan; the fix already exists as a platform feature (atomic immutable deploys), it just isn't documented as Solen's answer, so a future incident wastes the response window relearning Netlify's UI instead of clicking one button.
findings.local_evidence: netlify.toml has no comment mentioning rollback, deploy history, or 'if a deploy breaks prod.' _rules/CODE_SAFETY.md Rule 6 ('NO DEPLOY-WAIT RITUAL') and Rule 29 ('POST-EXECUTION SMOKE TEST') both describe what to do BEFORE/AFTER a normal deploy but neither mentions what to do when a deploy is already live and broken.
findings.absence_proof: grep -rli 'rollback' across _backend-system, _docs, _rules, _design-system, CLAUDE.md, ~/.claude/*.md, and both hooks directories surfaced only: DB compensating-transaction code (lib/bookings/issue-refund.ts, tests/lib/bookings/issue-refund.test.ts), migration-technique discussion (_backend-system/research/migrations.md section 1, framed as 'never write a down migration', not a deploy-revert plan), and unrelated booking-report/reschedule route names. Zero hits for a documented Netlify-deploy-revert procedure anywhere in the estate.
findings.existing_coverage: none for the web-deploy half. The migrations.md research file (section 1, point 8) DOES cover the DB half well ('fix forward, or restore from a full backup for a genuine disaster') and that belongs to the migrations domain, not duplicated here; the gap this finding names is specifically the Netlify code-deploy revert, which has no equivalent anywhere.
findings.where_it_should_live: a short new section in _rules/CODE_SAFETY.md or a new _rules/RELEASE.md, three lines: what broke, the button to press, what to check after.
findings.enforcement: checklist (doc-only); this is a one-time knowledge gap, not a machine-testable behavior, so a gate is the wrong tool here.

findings.title: The mobile-contract tripwire (npm run smoke) is not wired into CI at all
findings.principle: A test script written to catch a NAMED historical failure mode (here: PostgREST silently returning null instead of erroring on a renamed/missing column) must be added to a CI workflow in the same commit that creates it, or it does not count as protection, only as a manual habit that will be forgotten.
findings.why: scripts/api-smoke.ts's own header says it exists specifically because 'PostgREST silently swallows a .select() on a renamed/missing column,' which is this project's documented #1 silent-failure mode (also called out in the project CLAUDE.md's Silent no-ops section); a script built to catch that failure mode but never run automatically catches it only on the days someone remembers to type `npm run smoke`.
findings.local_evidence: package.json defines `"smoke": "tsx scripts/api-smoke.ts"`. grep across all 5 files in .github/workflows/ for the string 'smoke' or 'api-smoke' returns zero matches. The script itself (scripts/api-smoke.ts, read in full for the top ~80 lines) does live-DB zod-shape checks against 10 GET endpoints, exactly the kind of thing a schema-drift PR would silently break.
findings.absence_proof: grep -rn 'smoke\|api-smoke' .github/workflows/*.yml -> no output. Confirmed the only 'test'/'e2e' references in CI are the vitest `test` job and the gated `e2e` job (finding 01); smoke is absent from both.
findings.existing_coverage: none in CI. Fully built and working as a standalone script.
findings.where_it_should_live: add a `smoke` job to .github/workflows/quality.yml, same secrets-gated pattern as the existing `e2e`/`visual` jobs (it already needs live-DB read access, which the same 3 Supabase secrets already satisfy, no new secret required unlike the `e2e` job).
findings.enforcement: gate: wire it into quality.yml; since it only needs the 3 secrets already configured (per the verified `gh secret list` output), this one is immediately activatable, no owner action needed first.

findings.title: 21 disposable 'kill-test' scripts outnumber the 6 real regression tests 3.5-to-1, with no lifecycle rule
findings.principle: A verification script is either a REGRESSION TEST (lives under tests/ or e2e/, runs in CI on every push, and its failure blocks a merge) or a KILL-TEST (a one-off script written to prove a specific fix during a specific hardening sprint). A kill-test that is not deleted within 30 days of the sprint that created it must be either promoted into tests/ with a CI wiring, or deleted; it may not be left indefinitely in scripts/ pretending to be a safety net.
findings.why: The system prompt's own starting estimate of '29 test files' is only true if you count these 21 scripts as tests; they are not, they are single-run manual verification tools (their own names are literally 'ring1-kill-test', 'ring8b-kill-test'), so treating them as coverage overstates the real regression-protected surface by roughly 3.5x and hides how thin the actual safety net (6 vitest files) really is.
findings.local_evidence: `find scripts -iname '*test*' -o -iname '*kill*'` lists 21 files: ring1 through ring9 (with a/b/c/d suffixes) kill-test scripts, db-backup-kill-test.ts, spend-path-kill-test.ts, plus 2 non-kill-test scripts. None of them are referenced by any file in .github/workflows/ (grep confirmed no 'ring' or 'kill-test' string in any workflow YAML). scripts/e2e-booking.ts's own header even names the same pattern explicitly: 'same pattern as scripts/ring5d-kill-test.ts / scripts/spend-path-kill-test.ts', i.e. the pattern is acknowledged as a family, just never formalized with a keep-or-delete rule.
findings.absence_proof: grep -rn 'kill-test\|ring1\|ring2\|ring3\|ring5\|ring7\|ring8\|ring9' .github/workflows/ -> zero matches. grep -rli 'kill.test' _rules _backend-system CLAUDE.md -> zero matches for any lifecycle/retention policy on these scripts.
findings.existing_coverage: none. The scripts are useful artifacts of past hardening work (ring1 through ring9 map to a real remediation sprint) but nothing says whether they're expected to still pass, whether anyone re-runs them, or when they can be deleted.
findings.where_it_should_live: a short paragraph in _rules/CODE_SAFETY.md or vitest.config.ts's own header comment, defining the kill-test-vs-regression-test split and the 30-day promote-or-delete rule.
findings.enforcement: checklist for now (a CI job that flags any scripts/*-kill-test.ts file older than 30 days is easy to build later, but at this scale a documented rule plus an occasional manual sweep is proportionate); trigger to build the automated gate: once a THIRD kill-test-vs-real-test confusion incident happens, or once scripts/ exceeds ~30 such files.

findings.title: Feature flags have no lifecycle rule; a genuinely dead flag already exists in the code today
findings.principle: Every feature flag falls into exactly one of two categories at creation time, named in its `feature_flags.description` column: PERMANENT (an operational kill switch like maintenance_mode/bookings/payments, never removed) or LAUNCH (a temporary gate on a specific feature rollout). A LAUNCH flag that has sat at a single value (fully on or fully off) for more than 90 days with no active experiment must be deleted from both the code (`checkFeatureEnabled` call sites removed) and the `feature_flags` table row, in the same PR that makes the decision permanent.
findings.why: An un-removed flag is a silent branch nobody tests: the code path behind a permanently-false flag rots (no CI coverage exercises it), and a future reader cannot tell from the code alone whether the flag is still a live decision point or a scar from a launch that finished a year ago.
findings.local_evidence: lib/feature-flags.ts:10 defines `CLIENT_FEATURE_FLAGS.isMassageSpaEnabled: false` with the comment 'Phase 1: Hide Massage & Spa category.' grep across the entire repo (excluding node_modules) for `isMassageSpaEnabled` returns exactly ONE hit: its own definition. It is read nowhere. This is a fully dead flag sitting in production source with zero lifecycle rule that would have caught it. Separately, the DB-backed `FeatureKey` union in the same file lists 17 keys (bookings, payments, messaging, reviews, registration, last_minute, maintenance_mode, visual_editor, nail_features, barber_features, spa_features, discovery, dispute_reporting, upcharge_requests, vouchers, salon_of_month, referral) mixing clearly-permanent kill switches with clearly-temporary launch gates (nail_features has been false since migration 072, referral/twint/salon_of_month were all added within the same week in July as one-time launch flags) with no field distinguishing the two kinds.
findings.absence_proof: grep -rni 'flag.*lifecycle|remove.*flag|flag.*debt|stale.*flag|flag.*cleanup|sunset.*flag' across _backend-system, _docs, _rules, _design-system, CLAUDE.md, and ~/.claude/*.md returns zero hits for any removal/lifetime rule. The only adjacent rule found, _rules/I18N_ROUTING.md:62 ('use a feature flag instead of deleting code when removing something for now'), tells you how to ADD a flag, never when to remove one.
findings.existing_coverage: partial: the system is otherwise mature (an admin UI at app/api/admin/feature-flags/route.ts with RLS, audit logging via logAuditEvent, and a real dashboard page), it just has no removal criterion.
findings.where_it_should_live: supabase/migrations/028_feature_flags.sql's schema (add a `flag_type text CHECK (flag_type IN ('permanent','launch'))` column, or simpler: a `review_by date` column) plus a short LAW row in _backend-system or CLAUDE.md's design contract table.
findings.enforcement: checklist now (delete isMassageSpaEnabled in the next cleanup pass); gate later: once the flags table crosses ~25 rows, a CI script that reads `feature_flags.updated_at` for launch-type rows unchanged past 90 days and opens a warning is proportionate.

findings.title: The 'done means' checklist that exists (CODE_SAFETY.md Rule 29) is a self-check for an agent, not a release gate before code reaches production
findings.principle: Before any change that touches a money-path route (bookings, payments, refunds, disputes, walk-in pay, Stripe webhook) reaches `main`, the PR must show evidence of one of: (a) a passing vitest file exercising the changed lib function, or (b) a manually-run `npm run smoke`/`npm run e2e` output pasted into the PR description, or (c) an explicit one-line note naming why neither applies. Silence on this point is not an acceptable state for a money-path change.
findings.why: _rules/CODE_SAFETY.md Rule 29 ('POST-EXECUTION SMOKE TEST') is real and used, but every one of its 9 checks (build passes, tsc clean, files imported, feature-flag row exists, admin path allow-listed, translations present) is a code-correctness check the AGENT runs on itself before telling the owner 'done' -- none of the 9 checks asks 'did a test actually exercise the new money logic.' It is necessary and already followed, but it is not the release gate the FLOORS/taste system has for design (the verifier-PASS loop); no equivalent PASS/FAIL gate exists for backend money-path changes before they merge.
findings.local_evidence: _rules/CODE_SAFETY.md lines 218-231 (Rule 29's 9-item list) contain zero reference to running tests, vitest, or scripts/api-smoke.ts. Compare to the vitest suite that DOES exist (tests/lib/bookings/*.test.ts, tests/lib/purchases/issue-purchase-refund.test.ts): nothing connects 'I changed lib/bookings/issue-refund.ts' to 'therefore its test must have run and passed before I say done.'
findings.absence_proof: grep -n 'checklist\|done' _rules/CODE_SAFETY.md surfaces only Rule 29's own heading and the numbered items already quoted; no cross-reference to tests/ or vitest anywhere in the file.
findings.existing_coverage: partial: CI's `test` job (npx vitest run, quality.yml) DOES block a PR if an existing test fails, which is real and valuable. The gap is narrower: nothing forces a NEW money-path lib function to get a NEW test before merge; the ratchet only protects functions that already had a test written for them in the past.
findings.where_it_should_live: add a 10th item to CODE_SAFETY.md Rule 29, or a PR template checkbox, naming the money-path lib directories (lib/bookings/, lib/purchases/, lib/walkin/) that require a companion vitest file.
findings.enforcement: checklist today (a PR template line); gate later once headcount > 1, when a CI diff-based check ('a file under lib/bookings/** changed with no matching tests/lib/bookings/** change') becomes worth the false-positive noise it will generate at 1-developer scale.

findings.title: No named flakiness policy for the visual regression suite, and no retries configured
findings.principle: Every automated test that can flake for a reason unrelated to the code under test (a visual regression test against live, data-driven salon content; font-rendering variance across machines) needs a written one-line policy: how many retries before a real failure is declared, who has authority to re-run vs investigate, and what counts as 'this needs a rebaseline' vs 'this is a real bug.' Zero is a valid retry count only if that is a stated decision, not an accident of never having set the field.
findings.why: playwright.config.ts already documents that these are 'data-driven pages' with a 1% pixel tolerance specifically because live salon data can shift the render, which is an admission that some flakiness is expected; without a stated retry/triage policy, the first flaky failure becomes an ad-hoc judgment call under time pressure, exactly the situation a written policy exists to avoid.
findings.local_evidence: playwright.config.ts sets `fullyParallel: false`, `workers: 1`, `maxDiffPixelRatio: 0.01`, and `animations: 'disabled'` (real, thoughtful anti-flake mitigations) but never sets a `retries` field (grep for 'retries' in the file returns nothing, meaning Playwright's default of 0 applies). e2e/visual/spine.spec.ts's own comment says 'data-driven pages, so a small tolerance + a rebaseline after legit [changes]' -- acknowledging flakiness risk without naming the response procedure.
findings.absence_proof: grep -n 'retries' playwright.config.ts -> no output. grep -rli 'flak' across _rules, _backend-system, _design-system, CLAUDE.md -> no hits for a flakiness policy (only unrelated matches, none found in this pass).
findings.existing_coverage: partial: the mitigations that exist (disabled animations, 1x device scale, single worker, 1% tolerance) are real anti-flake engineering; what's missing is only the retry count and the human triage step.
findings.where_it_should_live: playwright.config.ts itself (`retries: process.env.CI ? 2 : 0` is the standard Playwright pattern) plus a one-line comment on what a repeat-failure means.
findings.enforcement: checklist/config change; trivial to fix directly, does not need a gate.

findings.title: CI's visual/e2e jobs test a `next start` process inside GitHub Actions, never the actual Netlify-built artifact
findings.principle: A CI check that claims to validate 'the site' must run against the same build runtime the site is actually served by, or its name must say so. Since Solen deploys via `@netlify/plugin-nextjs` (a wrapper that changes how routing, ISR, and edge/serverless functions are packaged versus plain `next start`), a CI job that runs `npm run build && npx next start` is validating a DIFFERENT artifact than what Netlify serves, and a pass there is not proof the live site works.
findings.why: Netlify's Next.js runtime plugin can diverge from vanilla `next start` behavior (different function splitting, different caching semantics), a divergence the project's OWN research file already flags generally (see existing_coverage); a CI green check that never touches that plugin cannot catch a Netlify-runtime-specific regression before it reaches the 28 live salons.
findings.local_evidence: .github/workflows/quality.yml's `visual` job: 'next build' then 'npx next start -p 3001' (no netlify-cli, no `netlify build`/`netlify dev`, no @netlify/plugin-nextjs invocation) then runs Playwright against that local process. netlify.toml's only plugin is `@netlify/plugin-nextjs`, which never runs in this CI job.
findings.absence_proof: grep -n 'netlify' .github/workflows/quality.yml -> no output; the word 'netlify' does not appear anywhere in the workflow file that builds and serves the app for testing.
findings.existing_coverage: partial: _backend-system/research/api-design.md:229 already flags the adjacent risk generally ('any Next.js caching/ISR/edge-function advice sourced from a Vercel-authored blog post needs re-verification against Netlify's actual adapter behavior... this file did not independently re-verify Netlify's Next.js plugin caching semantics'), but that is about not trusting outside ADVICE, not about the CI pipeline's own test artifact mismatch, which is the narrower and more concrete gap named here.
findings.where_it_should_live: the `visual` job in .github/workflows/quality.yml; Netlify offers a `netlify build` / `netlify-cli` local-runtime mode that can replace the bare `next start` step at low cost.
findings.enforcement: checklist for now, low urgency at 28 salons and a small Next.js surface; trigger to fix: the first time a bug ships that only reproduces under the Netlify runtime and not under `next start` (i.e. the first real incident this gap causes).

findings.title: The good instinct already in the test suite (money-path-only unit tests) is not written down as a rule, so nothing stops a future session from inventing a coverage mandate or skipping a new money function
findings.principle: At Solen's current scale (1 developer, ~28 salons, pre-launch), the ENTIRE required unit-test surface is: every function under lib/bookings/**, lib/purchases/**, and lib/walkin/** that moves money or changes booking/slot state gets a companion vitest file proving it does the mutation correctly under at least one success and one failure case. Nothing else needs a unit test: no UI component, no route handler wrapper, no percentage coverage target. This expands only when a stated trigger fires (a second paid engineer joins, OR transaction volume crosses roughly 50 bookings/day, OR a money-path bug ships to production that a unit test would have caught), never on a vague 'we should have more tests' feeling.
findings.why: The 6 existing vitest files already embody exactly this instinct (they cover issue-refund, customer-cancel-money, dispute-engine, off-session-charge, charge-fee, issue-purchase-refund, i.e. every money-mutating lib chokepoint that existed at the time), which is the correct testing pyramid for this scale; the risk is that this is tribal knowledge from one commit (ed5cf0557) rather than a stated rule, so the next money-path lib file added has nothing forcing its test to exist, and a future session under time pressure has no written floor to point to when deciding whether a full page-level test suite is warranted (it is not, yet).
findings.local_evidence: tests/lib/ contains exactly: charge-fee.test.ts, customer-cancel-money.test.ts, dispute-engine.test.ts, issue-refund.test.ts, off-session-charge.test.ts (all lib/bookings/), and issue-purchase-refund.test.ts (lib/purchases/); commit ed5cf0557's own message says '74 money-path tests (6 libs, mutation-proven to bite)', explicitly scoping to money-path. Meanwhile lib/bookings/ has 16 total files and only 6 have tests; the other 10 (claim-slot.ts, notify-refund.ts, reference.ts, notify-no-show-fee.ts, auto-assign.ts, guest-access.ts, authorize.ts, refund-config.ts, notify-upcharge.ts) are either notification/read-only helpers (correctly untested) or auto-assign.ts/authorize.ts/claim-slot.ts, which DO mutate slot/booking state and arguably belong in the same money-path tier but have no test today.
findings.absence_proof: grep -n 'test.*pyramid\|testing.*strategy\|coverage.*target' across _rules, _backend-system, CLAUDE.md, vitest.config.ts -> vitest.config.ts's header comment (read in full) states the WHAT ('pure-logic unit tests for the money-path lib/ chokepoints') but never states the boundary rule or the expansion trigger in writing anywhere else.
findings.existing_coverage: partial: vitest.config.ts's comment header is the closest thing to a stated scope, but it documents a technical config choice (why no `defineConfig` import), not the testing-philosophy rule itself, and it doesn't name claim-slot.ts/auto-assign.ts/authorize.ts as in-scope-but-missing.
findings.where_it_should_live: a short paragraph in CLAUDE.md's testing/CI section or a new _rules/TESTING.md, naming the exact scope boundary and the three expansion triggers.
findings.enforcement: behavioral rule for now (the boundary is a judgment call, not mechanically checkable); the concrete near-term action is adding tests for claim-slot.ts/auto-assign.ts/authorize.ts since they already meet the stated bar.

findings.title: The lint ratchet is frozen at 481 pre-existing errors with no glide path and no review trigger
findings.principle: A CI ratchet (a baseline that blocks NEW violations but grandfathers existing ones) must carry a stated re-evaluation trigger, not just a one-time number. For Solen's lint ratchet specifically: the baseline is reviewed and lowered by at least 10% whenever a developer is already touching a file with pre-existing lint errors in an unrelated change (fix-while-you're-there), and is hard-reviewed in full whenever the baseline itself would otherwise block an urgent fix.
findings.why: A ratchet that only ever holds a line and never moves it down is a permanent debt marker masquerading as a quality gate; 481 errors sitting untouched since the gate was created means the CI check has communicated 'these are all still fine' by omission for however long it's been live, and nobody has been asked to reduce them because the gate, by design, never asks.
findings.local_evidence: .github/workflows/quality.yml's `lint` job hardcodes `BASELINE=481` with the comment 'ratchet vs baseline, currently 481 pre-existing errors.' `git log --oneline -- .github/workflows/quality.yml` shows exactly one commit created this file (ed5cf0557) and one later commit (53c1890ea) that only touched the `typecheck`/`e2e`/`visual` jobs (moving tsc's baseline to 0 and adding e2e/visual); no commit has ever touched the lint job's BASELINE=481 line since it was created.
findings.absence_proof: grep -n 'BASELINE' .github/workflows/quality.yml shows two hardcoded numbers: `BASELINE=0` for tsc (already reached zero, good) and `BASELINE=481` for lint (never moved). No comment or doc anywhere states a plan or trigger to lower it.
findings.existing_coverage: partial: the tsc ratchet in the SAME file is a positive counter-example already proving this team CAN and DOES drive a ratchet to zero (tsc's comment: 'hard zero since 2026-07-11, the 4 pre-existing errors were fixed'), so the missing piece here is narrowly the lint side, not the whole pattern.
findings.where_it_should_live: the `lint` job's own comment in quality.yml, adding the same kind of 'reduce by N on next touch' note the tsc job effectively followed in practice.
findings.enforcement: checklist (a comment + a periodic manual sweep); a gate that auto-fails on baseline staying flat for N months is possible later but is overkill at 1-developer scale today.

findings.title: The Stripe webhook handler, the single most consequential untested route in the app, has zero test coverage
findings.principle: app/api/stripe/webhook/route.ts (912 lines: signature verification, event-type dispatch, and the terminal state transitions for every Stripe-driven booking/payment outcome) must have at least one test per handled Stripe event type proving: (a) an invalid/missing signature is rejected before any DB write, and (b) each event type drives the booking/payment row to the correct terminal state. This is narrower than 'test every route' -- it targets the one route where a silent bug means money moves or a booking's state diverges from Stripe's truth with no user-visible error to catch it.
findings.why: Every other money-mutating code path in this app (refund, cancel, dispute, off-session charge) already has a test proving the mutation is correct; the webhook route is the entry point that Stripe itself calls asynchronously with no human in the loop to notice a wrong response, making it the highest-consequence gap in the current money-path test set, not a generic 'add more tests' complaint.
findings.local_evidence: app/api/stripe/webhook/route.ts is 912 lines (wc -l, verified). find across the whole repo for any file matching '*webhook*test*' or '*test*webhook*' returns zero results. The 6 existing vitest files test the underlying lib/bookings/*.ts functions the webhook likely calls into (issue-refund.ts, off-session-charge.ts), but nothing tests the webhook route's OWN logic: signature verification, event-type routing, and idempotency on a replayed Stripe event.
findings.absence_proof: find . -iname '*webhook*test*' -o -iname '*test*webhook*' (excluding node_modules) -> no output. grep of tests/ directory listing shows only bookings/ and purchases/ subdirectories, no stripe/ or webhook/ subdirectory.
findings.existing_coverage: partial: the underlying money-movement functions the webhook likely calls (issue-refund, off-session-charge) are unit-tested in isolation; the webhook's own signature-verification and event-dispatch logic, and its idempotency behavior on a duplicate Stripe delivery, are not covered by any test at any layer.
findings.where_it_should_live: tests/api/stripe/webhook.test.ts, following the same vitest + node-environment pattern already established.
findings.enforcement: gate: this is a strong candidate to add to the vitest suite directly, since the infrastructure (vitest.config.ts, tests/helpers/supabase-stub.ts) already exists and only needs a new test file, not new tooling.
